📣Full Statement by SeaLight Director Ray Powell for yesterday's Saturday News Forum in Manila:

Thank you for having me. I’m Ray Powell, Executive Director of the SeaLight Foundation, a maritime transparency advocacy non-profit based in California.

I want to begin with a tribute to some personal heroes of mine, the officers and crew of the Philippine Coast Guard—and particularly of the BRP Suluan, whose change of command I attended Thursday. On August 11th last year, that crew held their course at Bajo de Masinloc while much larger Chinese navy and coast guard vessels bore down on them at high speed — and when those vessels collided with each other in the chase, the Suluan’s sailors immediately offered medical assistance.

I’d like to repeat something I said last year: the world has never witnessed a coast guard that has routinely demonstrated the courage, resilience, devotion to duty, professionalism and restraint that the men and women of the Philippine Coast Guard have displayed while standing up for their country's sovereign rights against overwhelming odds.

I raise this because the bravery of those sailors only makes sense when you understand the full scope of what they are up against. Beijing’s goal is not simply to control reefs and shoals in the West Philippine Sea. It is to convince the people of the Philippines to stop resisting — to accept Chinese control as a permanent fact of life. And for that, their campaign of maritime occupation depends on an equally aggressive campaign of political warfare right here in Manila.

For the past several months, SeaLight has been investigating the machinery that lies deep behind that campaign — a network of interlocking organizations all connected to the CCP’s United Front Work Department, and all operating here in the Philippines, though most Filipinos have never heard of them.

The connections are not a secret, but they are written in a language most Filipinos don’t use. They are in the organizations’ own publications, in Chinese state media or in the Chinese Embassy’s own press releases. We simply started reading what they wrote about themselves – in Mandarin.

We began at the center of the campaign, where the connections to the Chinese Communist Party were clearest and plainly spoken. The Philippine Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China is one of more than 200 councils worldwide controlled by the CCP’s United Front Work Department. Last October, the council held a regional forum here in Manila — 300 delegates, seven countries, congratulatory messages from Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office and twelve Chinese provincial governments, with the Chinese Embassy’s Chargé d’Affaires personally administering the new officers’ oath of office.

Among those in attendance was the chief editor of the United Daily News — one of Manila’s most prominent Chinese-language newspapers — who has simultaneously served as the council’s Secretary General since 2011. Nearly fifteen years, seven board terms, at least five different presidents.

That the editor of one of Manila’s oldest Chinese language news outlets is also the leader of its most important CCP-linked council is not an accident, because the Mandarin press has been one of Beijing’s most important conquests here in the Philippines. Our January investigation documented Ambassador Jing Quan summoning executives of eight Manila Mandarin outlets and telling them to “cooperate closely” with the embassy and “carry forward patriotism and love for the homeland.”

He was not talking about the Philippines.

It’s not just the media, however. Chinese-language education has also been a particular target of the CCP. Since 1991, the Philippine Chinese Education Research Center has run what Beijing calls the “Blood Transfusion Plan” — dispatching nearly 5,000 mainland Chinese teachers to the Philippines’ Chinese-language schools through a United Front-administered program.

Unsurprisingly, the center’s chairman, Huang Duanming, simultaneously holds a formal advisory position inside the reunification council. And it was he who signed a letter under his Filipino name, James Wang — requesting that public school classrooms be opened to a CCP-designed World War II anniversary essay contest encouraging Filipino children to frame Japan as an enemy and write about the “spirit of joint resistance.” That request – exploiting Philippine public school children for Beijing’s propaganda purposes – was approved, resulting in DepEd Regional Letter No. 107.

We published that story in The Diplomat two weeks ago.

I want to be very clear about something. This is not about stigmatizing the Chinese-Filipino community. Indeed, ethnic Chinese citizens worldwide are among the first victims of these United Front operations — their institutions infiltrated, their community organizations co-opted, their voices claimed by a foreign power that does not represent them. Our investigations don’t seek to target them – they target the hostile foreign state that seeks to take over those institutions and exploit them.

You might ask why a maritime transparency organization is investigating Mandarin newspapers and Chinese school curricula. The answer is that these are the heart of what analysts now call FIMI — foreign information manipulation and interference operations. Beijing doesn’t start its influence campaigns on social media or in English-language op-eds. It starts inside the Chinese-language institutions it has spent decades building or quietly taking control of, right here in Manila. The reunification council, the newspapers, the education center — these are its core infrastructure. Everything else radiates outward.

That is exactly why the embassy works so hard to silence anyone who looks too hard. Since January, it has issued eight official statements attacking SeaLight (and me) by name. Its ad hominem attacks have not disputed a single fact we’ve presented. It has done the same to its Philippine critics and investigators, such as the PCIJ and journalist Regine Cabato after their investigation into pro-China propaganda. The Committee to Protect Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, and the National Union of Journalists have all rallied to their defense.

I stand with PCIJ. I stand with Regine Cabato. I stand with all those who stand up to bullies and tell the truth without apology.

The Philippines already has a model for how to respond — its internationally celebrated maritime transparency campaign that made China’s aggression at sea visible to the world. The same principle applies to malign foreign influence. As my podcast co-host Jim Carouso and I argued last month in an op-ed for the Philippine Star, a foreign influence transparency law — similar to Australia's — that simply requires organizations resourced by or operating at the direction of a foreign government to declare it publicly.

The Philippine Coast Guard’s courage and devotion to duty is beyond reproach, but Beijing’s campaign to violate the Philippines’ sovereign rights does not end at the shoreline. Its gray zone campaign at sea is tightly linked to its political warfare campaign here in Manila. Fighting back begins with clearly recognizing the threat.

Thank you. I’m happy to take your questions.

@PCIJdotOrg @RegineCabato @coastguardph @diplomat @GordianKnotRay @PhilstarNews #Philippines #China #CCP @pressfreedom
